subject: Agriculture
title: Coffee Rust in Ceylon
description: A quick, practical guide to Coffee Rust in Ceylon.

hook.text: Ceylon (Sri Lanka) was the world's top coffee exporter in 1870. Within 20 years, not a single coffee tree remained.

buildup.text: Coffee rust fungus—Hemileia vastatrix—appeared in 1869, producing orange spores under every leaf.

discovery.text: The fungus blocked photosynthesis. Trees defoliated, stopped producing berries, and died within a few seasons.

twist.text: Planters ripped out coffee and planted tea instead. That's why Sri Lanka is famous for tea, not coffee.

climax.text: Coffee rust is still the most damaging coffee disease worldwide—costing $1 billion annually in Latin America.

punchline.text: A fungus turned a coffee island into a tea island. Disease rewrites economies.

quiz.question: Why did Sri Lanka switch from coffee to tea production?
options: Coffee rust destroyed all coffee trees, forcing planters to switch

details.summary: Coffee leaf rust caused by the fungus Hemileia vastatrix destroyed the entire coffee industry of Ceylon (Sri Lanka) in the 1870s-1880s. The epidemic forced planters to switch to tea, making Sri Lanka the tea-growing nation it is today and launching the science of plant pathology.
details.whyItMatters: The Ceylon coffee rust epidemic was the first well-documented crop disease disaster of the industrial age. It transformed an entire nation's economy and inspired some of the earliest scientific research into plant diseases.
takeaways: Coffee leaf rust destroyed Ceylon's entire coffee industry within about 15 years
Planters replaced coffee with tea, establishing Sri Lanka as a major tea producer
The epidemic prompted the first scientific study of plant diseases by Harry Marshall Ward

faq.question: How did coffee rust destroy Ceylon's coffee industry?
faq.answer: Hemileia vastatrix produces orange spores that infect coffee leaves, causing them to drop prematurely. Without leaves, trees cannot photosynthesize and produce beans. The fungus spread rapidly across Ceylon's plantations in the 1870s, and by the 1890s coffee production had collapsed entirely.

faq.question: What was the lasting impact of the Ceylon coffee rust epidemic?
faq.answer: Ceylon's planters switched to tea, transforming the island into one of the world's great tea producers. The disaster also launched scientific plant pathology—Harry Marshall Ward's research on the fungus in the 1880s was pioneering work in understanding how plant diseases spread.
